name: Remington IPL home device
lead: Remington sells home intense pulsed light (IPL) hair-removal devices under its iLight line. People use them to reduce unwanted body or facial hair at home so skin stays smoother for longer than with shaving, with repeated sessions because only follicles in the growth phase respond.[1]

IPL uses broad-spectrum light absorbed by melanin in the hair to heat and damage the follicle.[1] Wikipedia cites Remington as stating that IPL and laser devices should be used only on light to medium skin tones and work best on darker hair; the article presents this as a manufacturer claim.[1] Laser-hair-removal literature notes that dark, coarse hair on light skin responds best and that most people need at least eight treatments spaced weeks apart.[3]

Remington is an American personal-care brand whose history runs from 1937 electric shavers, through ownership by Sperry Rand, Victor Kiam in 1979 and Vestar, to Rayovac, later Spectrum Brands, in 2003.[2] No clinical trials of this specific device were found.

paras: Light is absorbed by melanin in the hair shaft and follicle, heating the structure that produces hair. Visible removal generally takes multiple sessions weeks apart.[1] Unlike lasers, IPL uses non-coherent light with filters to choose wavelengths.[1][3]

Evidence for IPL comes from clinic-grade systems. A 2006 study cited by Wikipedia reported about 67 percent hair reduction at six months, and a randomized trial cited on the laser hair removal page reported 52.7 percent reduction with IPL versus 69.2 percent with a diode laser at 12 months.[1][3] These studies did not test Remington devices.

Reported effects of light-based hair removal include redness, swelling, itching, burns and pigment changes; photosensitising medications and sunburned skin are listed as contraindications.[1][3] Manufacturer guidance limits use to lighter skin tones.[1] Hair removal lasers have been FDA-cleared for permanent hair reduction since 1997, and as of 2025 the FDA had cleared two diode laser devices for over-the-counter sale.[3]
No studies found for this device. Studies of clinic IPL systems are summarised above.[1][3]

card.summary: Remington's home IPL flasher: reduces hair over repeated sessions on light-to-medium skin, no device-specific trials.
card.note: Manufacturer limits use to light-to-medium skin tones.

quick.overview:
A consumer IPL device that flashes broad-spectrum light to damage hair follicles over multiple sessions.

Evidence for IPL exists for clinic systems; none was found for this specific device.
quick.mechanism: Melanin in the hair absorbs the light and heats the follicle; only growing hairs respond, so sessions are repeated.
quick.risks: Burns, redness and pigment changes are reported with light-based removal; the manufacturer limits use to lighter skin tones.

angle.text: A person flashes the device over areas such as legs, underarms or the bikini line, aiming for progressively thinner, slower-growing hair and smoother skin between sessions.
